title: DCL
description: Reason about grants, revocation, roles, and least privilege through explicit action/resource contracts, with synthetic permission audits kept separate from actual database enforcement.
notes:
## Describing authority rather than just valid syntax

Data Control Language, commonly called DCL, concerns the database capabilities assigned to accounts and roles. GRANT supplies a supported privilege or role relationship. REVOKE removes a specified assignment. The practical question is which identity may perform which operation on which resource. A statement that is syntactically correct can still be forbidden to the caller, and an authenticated connection does not automatically have authority over every object.

This topic uses MySQL 8.4 terminology. Names and permission ledgers are fictional teaching examples. The exercises read synthetic rows describing a policy; they do not create users, assign actual roles, or alter server privileges. Evaluating a model of authority is useful practice, but it must not be reported as verification of a production account or hosted security boundary.

Consider a reporting service whose task is reading permitted employee information. That requirement is narrower than saying the service needs database access. It does not require inserting employees, dropping tables, or delegating rights. Write the needed action and resource scope first, then compare the effective capability to that requirement rather than granting everything until the application happens to work.

## Separating identity, operation, and scope

Authentication establishes an identity under the system's supported mechanism. Authorization determines what that identity may do. Knowing the identifier of an employee or supplying it in a request proves neither ownership nor permission. Database privileges and trusted application checks can both contribute to the final access boundary, depending on the actual design.

A useful access description names the principal, action, and resource. The principal can be an account or role. The action can be SELECT or UPDATE. The resource can be a particular object or another supported scope. A table-level reporting requirement is different from a database-wide privilege, even when both permit today's one report to run.

Record scope also matters. A capability to read an object does not inherently implement a product rule that a teacher sees only their own students. Hiding other rows in a browser is insufficient when a broader query path remains available. Trace the trusted query and database mechanisms that actually restrict the actor's accessible population.

## Understanding the effect of a narrow grant

Assume an administrator has already reviewed a role called report_reader. The following MySQL syntax illustrates assigning a table-level reading capability. It is explanatory text rather than a command executed by this rebuild.

```sql
GRANT SELECT ON training.employees TO 'report_reader';
```

The assignment concerns SELECT on the named object. It does not itself grant every operation, and it does not prove that the role or its users have no other capabilities. An old direct UPDATE grant or another active role can still contribute authority. A new narrow statement cannot be read as a complete inventory of existing permissions.

Account and role names also have their own supported syntax and administrative ownership. Do not construct privileged statements by concatenating unrestricted user input. A correctly quoted resource name is still only a name; it does not establish that the proposed assignment is appropriate or that the current actor is authorized to make it.

## Applying least privilege to a concrete task

Least privilege gives an identity the capabilities its task needs while avoiding unnecessary authority. It is not a rule to deny every operation until the application becomes unusable. Begin with required behavior, identify the trusted enforcement point, and verify that intended work succeeds while prohibited work fails under the relevant identity and context.

Broad ALL PRIVILEGES assignments can hide the original missing requirement and widen the consequences of a defect. They also make later investigation harder because successful execution no longer reveals which rights were necessary. A temporary debugging convenience can become a permanent unexplained dependency if nobody traces and removes the excess authority through the approved process.

A reading capability can still expose sensitive information or consume substantial resources. Least privilege reduces certain potential effects; it does not prevent SQL injection by itself or make every permitted read harmless. Safe input construction, record authorization, and operational limits remain separate controls that must be assessed at their own boundaries.

## Grouping responsibilities with roles

A role collects privileges that can be assigned and reviewed together. A reporting role, an editing role, and a maintenance role can reflect distinct tasks. Grouping reduces repeated administration, but it also creates paths through which an account obtains capability. Reviewing only direct grants can miss authority supplied through an applicable role.

MySQL role assignment and role activation are distinct concepts. Do not assume every assigned role is active in every session. Default-role settings and supported activation behavior need review in the real environment. The synthetic exercise uses an explicit active flag so its small policy is clear; it does not reproduce every feature of the MySQL role subsystem.

Real role relationships can also involve inheritance and administrative options. A full audit must account for relevant paths and scope. The classroom model deliberately excludes nested roles, global rights, and delegation. This restriction makes the exercise understandable while leaving those real-engine questions explicitly unverified rather than silently assuming they do not exist.

## Interpreting revocation accurately

REVOKE removes the specified assignment. It is not a universal prohibition that overrides every other path to the same action. If an account receives SELECT directly and through an active role, removing the direct grant can leave reading available through the role. Trace effective capability before announcing that access has been removed.

The timing of privilege changes also depends on product and privilege category. Do not promise that every revocation immediately terminates an already open session. Check the exact supported behavior and any approved operational steps needed for the intended result. The tutorial does not disconnect live sessions or claim to observe hosted permission changes.

Denied-operation tests need the correct cause. A query that fails because a table does not exist has not proved a privilege restriction on the intended object. Likewise, a successful read does not prove that all prohibited writes fail. Real enforcement evidence requires the intended identity, resource, operation, and context rather than merely any error or success message.

## Auditing an explicit teaching ledger

A synthetic assigned_rights table can list a principal, object, and action. Suppose report_reader needs only SELECT on employees. A query can find an unexpected UPDATE on employees or a SELECT on payroll. The result identifies assignments outside the stated requirement, without issuing an actual privilege statement.

A richer fixture can contain direct rights, active memberships, role rights, and requested operations. Its explicit rule allows a request when either a matching direct capability exists or an active role supplies the same object and action. Existence tests preserve one decision per request when two paths both allow it. Joining every matching path naively can instead duplicate the decision row.

Inserting a ledger row saying SELECT does not give the connection running the exercise that privilege. A computed denied result means no path exists under the fixture's defined policy. It does not mean the actual database rejected an operation for a real user. Preserve this distinction in explanations and verification records so simulation is not mistaken for enforcement.

## Keeping access contracts current

Application responsibilities change. A former editing service can become read-only while retaining an obsolete writing role. Review required behavior and effective authority together, then use the approved administrative process for changes. Removing an editor button alone does not remove a database capability already assigned to the service identity.

Keep credentials and private account data out of fixtures, comments, and diagnostic output. Use fictional names and approved references. A permission investigation that exposes a connection secret has crossed another sensitive boundary while trying to inspect access. Reproducibility should come from bounded evidence and explicit assumptions rather than copied production credentials.

DCL makes authority an explicit contract. Narrow assignments, clear role paths, and precise revocation claims support reviewable permission reasoning. Synthetic audits can teach that reasoning safely, while actual allowed and denied operations still require authorized checks against the real engine, identities, and trusted enforcement mechanisms.

questions.question_text: Which two verbs form the core of DCL?
options: CREATE and DROP
GRANT and REVOKE
COMMIT and ROLLBACK
SELECT and INSERT
questions.explanation: GRANT and REVOKE manage permissions — the essence of DCL.

questions.question_text: What does a narrow SELECT grant establish by itself?
options: It deletes all employee data
The specified reading capability, while other effective rights still require review
It creates a new table called app_readonly_role
It removes all permissions from app_readonly_role
questions.explanation: A new narrow grant does not erase older direct or role-derived authority.

questions.question_text: What is the 'principle of least privilege' that DCL is meant to implement?
options: Every account should be granted every possible privilege by default
Each account should have exactly the permissions it needs to do its job, and no more
Privileges should be granted randomly to test the system
Only the database administrator should ever be able to log in
questions.explanation: Least privilege means scoping each account's access as narrowly as its actual job requires.

questions.question_text: Why might granting ALL PRIVILEGES broadly 'to make things work' be a bad long-term habit?
options: It has no downsides and is always the correct approach
It defeats least privilege and makes it much harder to reason about what an over-privileged account can't do, increasing the blast radius of any bug or attack
ALL PRIVILEGES is not valid SQL syntax
It only affects DDL statements, not DML
questions.explanation: Over-granting privileges widens the potential damage from a bug or compromised credential, which is exactly what least privilege tries to prevent.

questions.question_text: Why avoid unnecessary write authority for a reading report?
options: Because SELECT is the only privilege that exists in SQL
It reduces unneeded write capability while confidentiality and resource risks still need controls
Because SELECT is required before any other GRANT can be issued
Because dashboards cannot connect to databases that support INSERT
questions.explanation: Reading is not universally harmless; least privilege is one boundary.

questions.question_text: In many database systems, what is a 'role' in the context of DCL?
options: A synonym for a single specific user account
A named bundle of privileges that can be granted to users as a unit, rather than granting many individual privileges one at a time
A type of table constraint
A kind of index
questions.explanation: Roles group privileges together so they can be assigned and managed as a single unit, which scales better than per-user, per-privilege grants.

questions.question_text: Does REVOKE-ing a privilege necessarily terminate an already-open session immediately on every database engine?
options: Yes, always, instantly, on every engine with no exceptions
Not necessarily — how and when a revoked privilege takes effect for an already-open session can vary by engine
REVOKE never has any effect on open sessions, ever
REVOKE only works if the user is currently disconnected
questions.explanation: The timing of when a REVOKE actually takes effect for an existing session is engine-dependent — an important operational subtlety.

questions.question_text: Assuming no other effective rights, what bounds a compromised connection with SELECT and INSERT on two objects?
options: The impact is identical to full database access, since DCL provides no real protection
Its effective privileges limit the operations and objects available, although allowed reads and inserts can still cause harm
The application becomes completely unusable the moment it is compromised
DCL prevents SQL injection from ever succeeding in the first place
questions.explanation: Least privilege does not prevent injection or make permitted operations safe in every context.

questions.question_text: What must be distinguished from authentication?
options: The existence of a principal
Authorization for a specific action and resource
The identity established by a connection
The fact that credentials were accepted
questions.explanation: Authentication alone does not supply every capability.

questions.question_text: Does removing one direct grant always remove the action supplied through a role?
options: Yes; every role disappears
Only when the table is empty
No; the surviving role path needs review
Only when the name is lowercase
questions.explanation: Effective rights can have several paths.

questions.question_text: A report needs SELECT on employees only. Which assignment is excessive?
options: SELECT on employees
The stated requirement
UPDATE on employees
The reporting identity
questions.explanation: Writing is outside the stated task.

questions.question_text: The fixture has no direct grant but an active role supplies the requested object and action. What is the decision?
options: Denied because only direct rights count
Allowed on every object
The request is removed
Allowed
questions.explanation: The defined policy accepts an active matching role path.

questions.question_text: A matching membership is inactive and no direct right exists. What is the fixture decision?
options: Denied
Allowed because assignment always means activation
Allowed for every action
The object becomes a role
questions.explanation: Only active memberships contribute under the stated rule.

questions.question_text: Two matching paths allow one request. How many decision rows should appear?
options: Two duplicate requests
One
No rows because paths cancel
One per unrelated role
questions.explanation: Existence preserves the request grain.

questions.question_text: One grant is revoked but an active role still supplies it. What claim is unsupported?
options: One assignment was removed
Effective paths matter
The account can no longer perform the action
The role can supply authority
questions.explanation: The surviving path may preserve the capability.

questions.question_text: A synthetic query returns denied. What remains unproved?
options: No fixture path matched
The policy query returned a row
Synthetic data was evaluated
Actual database rejection under a real account
questions.explanation: A policy model is distinct from engine enforcement.

questions.question_text: A browser filters a broadly readable sensitive table. What is unresolved?
options: Trusted restriction of the permitted record population
Only the font
Only the role caption
Only the display order
questions.explanation: Client filtering is not an independent access boundary.

questions.question_text: A test fails because the target table is missing. Does it prove privilege denial?
options: Yes; any error proves authorization
No; it failed for a different reason
Only if the message is red
Only if SELECT was used
questions.explanation: Evidence must identify the intended enforcement cause.

questions.question_text: A MySQL role is assigned. What still needs review for a current session?
options: Only its name length
Only report column count
Activation and default-role behavior
Only hostname spelling
questions.explanation: Assigned and active roles are different concepts.

questions.question_text: How should permission diagnostics refer to credentials?
options: Copy a real password into every fixture
Publish the connection string
Grant access to everyone
Use approved references without secret values
questions.explanation: Access investigations must preserve secret boundaries.

coding_problems.title: Audit a synthetic reader assignment
coding_problems.task: For principal report_reader, return object_name and privilege_name for synthetic assigned_rights rows other than the required SELECT on employees. Order by object_name then privilege_name. Do not issue GRANT or REVOKE. The ledger is not the server privilege catalog.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE assigned_rights (principal VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, object_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, privilege_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (principal,object_name,privilege_name));
coding_problems.expected:
object_name	privilege_name
employees	UPDATE
payroll	SELECT
edge_cases: Do not flag the required right
No assignments means no excess rows
hints: Exclude exactly the required object/action pair
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT object_name,privilege_name FROM assigned_rights WHERE principal='report_reader' AND NOT (object_name='employees' AND privilege_name='SELECT') ORDER BY object_name,privilege_name;
coding_problems.explanation: This compares assignment facts to the fixture requirement without mutating actual privileges or proving real account enforcement.

coding_problems.title: Evaluate direct and active-role paths
coding_problems.task: Return request_id and decision (allowed or denied) for each synthetic access_requests row. Allow an exact object/action match through direct_rights or through role_rights linked by memberships with active=1. Return one row per request ordered by request_id. Nested roles, global rights, delegation, and actual server grants are outside this model.
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO direct_rights VALUES ('Mira','employees','SELECT'); INSERT INTO memberships VALUES ('Mira','reader',1),('Dev','reader',0),('Noor','reader',1); INSERT INTO role_rights VALUES ('reader','employees','SELECT'); INSERT INTO access_requests VALUES (1,'Mira','employees','SELECT'),(2,'Dev','employees','SELECT'),(3,'Noor','employees','SELECT'),(4,'Noor','employees','UPDATE'),(5,'Mira','payroll','SELECT');
coding_problems.expected:
request_id	decision
1	allowed
2	denied
3	allowed
4	denied
5	denied
edge_cases: Wrong action or object does not match
hints: Use EXISTS rather than a multiplying join
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT q.request_id,CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM direct_rights d WHERE d.actor=q.actor AND d.object_name=q.object_name AND d.privilege_name=q.privilege_name) OR EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM memberships m JOIN role_rights r ON r.role_name=m.role_name WHERE m.actor=q.actor AND m.active=1 AND r.object_name=q.object_name AND r.privilege_name=q.privilege_name) THEN 'allowed' ELSE 'denied' END AS decision FROM access_requests q ORDER BY q.request_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The existence checks implement the declared synthetic policy without duplicate decisions. This is not verification of the actual database privilege system.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO memberships VALUES ('Avi','r1',1),('Avi','r2',1); INSERT INTO role_rights VALUES ('r1','employees','SELECT'),('r2','employees','SELECT'); INSERT INTO access_requests VALUES (7,'Avi','employees','SELECT');

Because SELECT is required before any other GRANT can be issued
Because dashboards cannot connect to databases that support INSERT
original_questions.explanation: Scoping the account to only what it functionally needs (reading) limits the worst-case impact of anything going wrong with that account.

original_questions.question_text: A web application is compromised via a bug that lets an attacker inject arbitrary SQL, but the app's database account only has SELECT and INSERT on two specific tables. What does DCL's design principle predict about the worst-case impact?
options: The impact is identical to full database access, since DCL provides no real protection
The damage is structurally limited to what SELECT/INSERT on those two tables allows — the attacker cannot DROP tables or read other tables the account was never granted access to
The application becomes completely unusable the moment it is compromised
DCL prevents SQL injection from ever succeeding in the first place
original_questions.explanation: Least-privilege DCL doesn't prevent every attack, but it limits the blast radius: an attacker is bounded by whatever privileges the compromised account actually holds.
